title.narrative: UNECE Promoting Innovation in Eastern Europe
UNECE Utveckling av innovationssystem i Östeuropa

description.narrative: The United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) has applied for funding from Sida of 2, 215, 026 USD to carry out the project "Promoting innovation policy capacities in Eastern Europe and the Caucasus" during the period 2018-2022. The intervention aims at improving competencies among innovation policy institutions in designing, running, reforming and monitoring effective innovation policies and institutions. This will be done through (1) the development and regional implementation of an innovation policy index, (2) the cunduct of Innovation Performance Reviews for Sustainable Development in Georgia, Moldova and Armenia and (3) targeted capacity building in Georgia and Moldova and on a regional level.

United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) har inkommit med en ansökan till Sida om 2, 215, 026 USD för genomförandet av projektet "Promoting innovation policy capacities in Eastern Europe and the Caucasus" under perioden 2018-2022. Insatsen syftar till stärkt kapacitet hos policyinstitut och beslutsfattare för att skapa, implementera, reformera och underhålla ett funktionellt regelverk och effektiva institutioner för innovation. Detta görs genom (1) utveckling och implementering av ett index för att mäta innovationspolicy, (2) genomförande av studier av nationella innovationssystem (Innovation Performance Reviews for Sustainable Development) i Georgien, Moldavien och Armenien, samt (3) riktade kapacitetsutvecklingsinsatser i bland annat Georgien, Moldavien samt på regional nivå.

"The project will improve the competencies of innovation policy makers in designing, running, reforming, and monitoring effective innovation policies and institutions that make measurable contributions towards long-term economic development and sustainable development." In this programme UNECE focus on Moldova, Armenia and Georgia.
Expected accomplishments EA1.Enhanced capacity of national policy makers and stakeholders to analyse and benchmark their innovation policies and institutions in line with ECE good practices. EA2. Enhanced capacity of national policy makers and stakeholders in three countries to design and carry out effective innovation policy and institutional reform. EA3. Improved subregional cooperation on harmonisation of innovation policies and institutions.
Indicators of achievement IA1.1. At least 3 countries endorsed the findings of the innovation policy index and the I4SD reviews and integrated relevant recommendations into their national policies. IA2.1. At least 80% of stakeholders beneflting from national capacity building confirmed that activities strengthened their capacity in designing, implementing, and evaluating effective innovative policy. IA3.l. At least 5 countries demonstrate that recommendations made in project activities and reflected in the policy handbook are reflected in ongoing or intended changes or reforms to policies, institutions, or instruments.

title.narrative: Agreement between Sweden and UNECE reg. contribution no. 12333

description.narrative:
According to the final narrative report, UNECE's activities has contributed to the following:
Armenia
Policy changes:
- The State Programme on the Development of the High-Tech Industry and Innovation Ecosystem was developed in 2024 and launched in May 2025 to support technology start-ups across all development stages. The design and priorities of the programme were informed by recommendations of the I4SDR for Armenia.
- Under the framework of the State Programme, the Government of Armenia institutionalised a strategic collaboration with the global accelerator Plug and Play Armenia to provide tailored mentorship, international networking and investor-linkage opportunities for Armenian start-ups.
Behavior changes:
- Public support for innovation in Armenia has shifted from dispersed, stand-alone grant schemes towards a more structured and sequenced approach under the State Programme. Support is now organised across distinct stages of start-up development, from incubation and early validation to acceleration and internationalisation, with clearer eligibility criteria, defined co-financing requirements, coordinated implementation with partners such as Plug and Play Armenia, and structured monitoring and follow-up mechanisms led by the Ministry of High-Tech Industry.
- International networking and cooperation with the global accelerator Plug and Play Armenia has helped start-ups access mentorship, investor networks and global market connections, encouraging them to meet international standards.
- Collaboration between government and start-ups has become more regular and structured. Coordination meetings, joint programme management and recurring events such as Demo Days and Investor Sessions have strengthened publicprivate dialogue and improved overall steering of the high-tech sector.
Outcomes:
- Increased pipeline of investment-ready start-ups, with more structured progression from idea-stage support to acceleration and international exposure, improving the quality and maturity of ventures entering regional and global markets.
- Strengthened access to finance, enhancing the capacity of Armenian technology firms to commercialise innovations, attract private capital and pursue export-oriented growth strategies.
- A more coherent, innovation-driven high-tech sector, reinforcing Armenias positioning within regional and global technology value chains.
Georgia
Policy changes:
- Formal recognition of public procurement as a strategic policy instrument with an innovation dimension: the Law of Georgia on Public Procurement adopted in February 2023, embeds sustainable development objectives within the purpose and principles of procurement and requires contracting authorities to consider innovation, environmental, social and economic aspects in purchasing decisions. This aligns closely with recommendations in the I4SDR of Georgia and the capacity building work on innovation enhancing procurement (IEP). By moving away from a strict lowest-price focus and allowing authorities to consider quality, performance and long-term value (not just cost), the law makes it easier for public bodies to buy innovative solutions instead of simply choosing the cheapest option. The revised legal framework also aligns with EU standards by strengthening transparency and review mechanisms. UNECE also supported the institutionalisation of innovation-oriented procurement through integration into State Procurement Agency's (SPA) regular training curriculum, reaching around 300 procurement specialists annually.
Behavior changes:
- Georgias Innovation & Technology Agency (GITA) and (SPA) shifted from compliance- and price-driven purchasing towards outcome-based procurement practices. The new approaches have progressively disseminated across line ministries and contracting authorities through updated guidance, pilot tenders and institutionalised training programmes. As a result, procurement is increasingly framed in terms of performance and problem-solving objectives rather than rigid technical specifications, reflecting a concrete behavioural shift in day-to-day practice from lowest-price logic towards results orientation.
- Procurement needs allowed suppliers to propose innovative approaches to meet environmental targets. In practice, this enabled enterprises to introduce resource-efficient and cleaner production technologies - reducing raw material use, energy consumption, waste and emissions - supported by Sustainable Public Procurement pilot tenders, which helped create market demand for greener industrial processes.
Outcomes:
- Demand for innovative solutions has increased, including testing and scaling up across sectors, generating more predictable demand for innovative SMEs and start-ups, incentivising enterprise investment in new and greener technologies, and strengthening procurement.
- Improved production efficiency, reducing resource use, lowering emissions and waste, and increasing productivity and competitiveness.
- Public procurement now supports Georgias transition towards a more innovation-driven and sustainability-oriented economy.
Moldova
Policy changes:
- The Roadmap on Innovation and Technology Transfer was developed in follow-up to the I4SDR, in response to recommendations and subsequent capacity building. It directly informed the design of the National Programme on Research and Innovation 2024 to 2027, which was approved by the Government of Moldova as the primary strategic framework guiding research, innovation and innovation ecosystem reforms for 2024 to 2027.
- The Roadmap translated strategic priorities on strengthening scienceindustry linkages and improving the commercialisation of research into a sequenced set of concrete actions. It included measures to strengthen technology transfer offices, standardise intellectual property management practices, introduce dedicated instruments for collaborative research, and clarify institutional responsibilities for supporting research commercialisation within the national innovation system.
Behavior changes:
- Research organisations and universities have formalised technology transfer practices, including the adoption of clearer internal procedures for intellectual property disclosure and management and the setting up/strengthening of technology transfer functions within institutions.
- The design of funding calls under the National Programme now incorporates eligibility criteria and evaluation elements favouring academiabusiness collaboration.
- Inter-institutional coordination has become more structured, with the Ministry of Education and Research and the National Agency for Research and Development aligning programme design, call documentation, and evaluation procedures.
Outcomes:
- Increased commercialisation activity of publicly funded research, with a growing number of research projects incorporating industry partners and market-oriented components.
- Stronger academiabusiness linkages have improved the relevance of research to enterprise needs, contributing to enhanced absorptive capacity in firms, greater uptake of research results by the private sector, and improved prospects for technology-based start-ups and spin-offs.
- A more coherent technology transfer framework has enhanced the valorisation of research outputs, supporting diversification of the innovation ecosystem and reinforcing Moldovas capacity to participate in international research and innovation programmes, including European partnerships.
Ukraine
Policy changes:
- Adoption of a strategic, recovery-oriented innovation framework under the WINWIN Innovation Strategy, which positions innovation as a driver of Ukraines recovery, aligning reconstruction efforts with green, digital and EU-integration priorities.
Behavior changes:
- Innovation governance is becoming more coordinated and strategic: the establishment of a dedicated WINWIN Project Office, with experts drawn from government, international partners and the private sector, is driving more systematic interaction between state institutions, businesses and external partners to implement projects across AI, agri-tech, med-tech and other activities.
- Broader stakeholder engagement: WINWIN has shifted the behaviour of public actors towards greater openness in collaboration with private innovators and international experts.
Outcomes:
- Enhanced competitiveness and establishment of flagship innovation infrastructure and collaborative platforms. Ukraine launched the WINWIN AI Center of Excellence and related initiatives, including partnerships with industry leaders such as NVIDIA and Kyivstar to develop national AI capabilities, demonstrating strategic progress in building high-impact innovation assets and cross-sector collaboration.
